body.text: On 26 August 2026, the ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) activated Alert Level 3, its highest haze alert, for southern ASEAN. Four days later, satellite imagery recorded 1,211 hotspots across the region, including 1,180 in Kalimantan.

What has changed is the technology. Earth observation satellites provide detailed information about fires and land conditions, while artificial intelligence (AI) can help identify patterns and forecast risks. But technology has rarely been the only missing piece. Each capability is useful only when paired with a governance arrangement that turns information into action.
From fire detection to risk forecasting

Satellites remain central to haze monitoring. Thermal instruments detect active fires several times a day, optical imagery maps burned areas, and radar sees through cloud and smoke. Yet detection helps only if someone is mandated to respond. Hotspot data must feed into agreed protocols specifying which agency verifies a fire, within what timeframe, and who deploys suppression teams.
Technology alone cannot make up for weak implementation, or the failure to hold those responsible for fires to account.

AI can go further by identifying where fires are likely to occur. A study used remote-sensing data and machine learning to predict forest fires in Indonesia. Combining water-table sensors, rainfall forecasts, satellite soil-moisture estimates, and radar observations could also flag degraded and drained peatlands becoming dangerously dry before hotspots appear. Such forecasts still need operational validation, and matter only if warnings compel action. Authorities need the legal mandate and resources to inspect flagged areas, require concession holders to rewet peat, and sanction those who do not.

A hotspot map cannot explain which communities face the greatest risks, where smoke will travel, or which interventions should come first. Projects such as MIT Media Lab’s Earth Mission Control and NASA’s VIIRS show how satellite data can be presented through interactive maps. Southeast Asian states could combine fire-risk forecasts, wind direction, and satellite imagery with the locations of communities, hospitals, and schools.

A shared picture, however, needs shared rules. States need to agree on alert thresholds that trigger specific responses, and on who issues public advisories when smoke crosses borders. These rules must be built around practical questions, such as which communities face smoke exposure and where prevention should come first, with local knowledge and human judgement kept central.

That said, AI models trained on historical data may struggle with extreme events beyond their training experience. AI-powered social media monitoring can overlook communities using local languages or lacking reliable internet access. And plausible but inaccurate outputs are dangerous when warnings must be fast. The governance response is to document model limitations and require designated officials to review AI-informed warnings before release.

Institutional fragmentation is harder to fix. Indonesian peat fire management has been spread across national, provincial, and village institutions, with no single body in charge. When the peat restoration agency’s mandate ended in 2024, its sensor network and expertise were handed to ministries and local authorities, and it is unclear how much of its coordination survives. A planned successor has yet to be established, while access to forest and fire data has been restricted.

Second, pool data and test. Indonesia can draw on the combined capacity of its neighbours, including ASMC in Singapore and other national space agencies in the region. Southeast Asian countries could then pool hotspot and burned-area datasets, peatland information, and advisory templates in regional languages, and test models against severe fire seasons.

Third, close the capacity gap. Better resourced ASEAN member states can offer training, satellite ground-station access, computing resources, and technical assistance through a regional shared-service model, while national agencies retain control over local data and operational decisions.

ASEAN’s goal of a haze-free region by 2030 requires more than technological infrastructure or advancement. Technology is unevenly distributed across the region, and many of the hardest problems are physical: blocking drainage canals, rewetting peat, and reaching fires in remote terrain.

Space and AI can show where action is needed, but only enforcement, accountability, and cross-border cooperation can ensure change happens. Technology alone cannot make up for weak implementation, or the failure to hold those responsible for fires to account.
Karryl Kim Sagun Trajano is a Research Fellow for Future Issues and Technology (FIT) at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS), Nanyang Technological University (NTU), Singapore.
